1F (Number Theory)

Words: 142 Articles: 1
Paper 2 OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 142
1F OurBigBook.com
Write p=8k+7. In Gauss's lemma, for the multiplier 2, precisely the integers j with p/4<j≤(p−1)/2 give residues 2j>p/2. Their number is
2p−1​−⌊4p​⌋=(4k+3)−(2k+1)=2k+2.
(1)
It is even, so the Legendre symbol (2/p)=1: 2 is a quadratic residue modulo p. For completeness, the sign rule follows by replacing those large residues by their negatives; the resulting absolute residues permute 1,…,(p−1)/2. Multiplying them and cancelling their nonzero product gives 2(p−1)/2≡(−1)2k+2=1(modp), equivalent to the residue assertion by Euler's criterion.
Now take the prime p=2q+1. The condition q≡3(mod4) gives p≡7(mod8), so 2q≡1(modp). Thus p divides 2q−1. For integers q>3, 2q−1>2q+1 (true at 4 and preserved on increasing q), so this divisor is proper and 2q−1 is composite. At q=3, the divisor is the number itself: 23−1=2⋅3+1=7. The congruence still holds, but it does not establish compositeness.

2F (Topics in Analysis)

Words: 136 Articles: 1
Paper 2 OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 136
2F OurBigBook.com
Choose a point of K with both coordinates positive, so its product is positive. The set K∩[0,∞)2 is nonempty and compact; the continuous function xy therefore attains its maximum there. A maximizer cannot lie on either axis, where the product is zero. It consequently belongs to K∩P+ and also maximizes the product on that set.
For uniqueness, the function Φ(x,y)=logx+logy is strictly concave on the positive quadrant: its Hessian is diag(−1/x2,−1/y2), negative definite. If two distinct positive points attained the same maximal product, their midpoint would belong to K∩P+ by convexity and strict concavity would give a larger value of Φ, hence a larger product. This contradiction proves existence and uniqueness of the positive product maximizer. This argument is positive-product maximization on a convex set; compactness should be applied to the closed quadrant intersection, not directly to the potentially noncompact set K∩P+.

3G (Geometry of Group Actions)

Words: 286 Articles: 1
Paper 2 OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 286
3G OurBigBook.com
Here a planar lattice means a discrete subgroup of the additive Euclidean plane; full rank is not required. Discreteness at zero gives an ϵ>0 such that distinct lattice points are at least ϵ apart. Consequently every bounded set contains only finitely many lattice points, by placing disjoint small disks around them. If the group is zero, it has the stated one-generator form with w=0.
Otherwise choose a shortest nonzero lattice vector w1​. Every lattice point on its line is an integer multiple: subtract the nearest integer multiple of w1​ from a putative noninteger multiple to obtain a nonzero shorter vector, a contradiction. This already proves the one-generator case when all lattice points lie on that line.
For the remaining case choose the perpendicular orientation so that some point has positive height above the line of w1​. Reduce its parallel component modulo w1​ into [0,∣w1​∣). Among reduced points of positive height there is a least height d>0. Indeed, heights tending to zero would give infinitely many points in a bounded strip, contrary to the finiteness just proved; bounded sets also ensure that a positive infimum is attained. Choose w2​ at height d.
Given any lattice vector v, subtract an integer multiple of w2​ so that its height lies in [0,d), then reduce its parallel component modulo w1​. Minimality of d forces the residual height to be zero, and the one-dimensional argument forces the residual to be an integer multiple of w1​. Therefore
Λ=Zw1​+Zw2​,w1​,w2​ linearly independent.​
(2)
Together with the rank-one and zero cases this proves the planar discrete-subgroup basis assertion. Under the alternative convention that a Euclidean lattice must have full rank, only the two-generator case is called a lattice.

4G (Coding and Cryptography)

Words: 179 Articles: 1
Paper 2 OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 179
4G OurBigBook.com
A digital signature lets the holder of a private key authenticate a message so that anyone with the corresponding trusted public key can verify its origin and integrity. The signature does not conceal the message. Public-key certification, a suitable message hash and protection of the signing key are needed for that interpretation.
For the ElGamal signature scheme, choose a large prime p and a primitive root g modulo p. The secret key is x, and the public key is (p,g,y) with y=gxmodp. Represent the message by a hash m modulo p−1. Choose a fresh secret nonce k coprime to p−1 and set
r=gkmodp,s=k−1(m−xr)mod(p−1).​
(3)
The signature is (r,s). After checking the prescribed ranges, the verifier accepts when
gm≡yrrs(modp).​
(4)
A genuine signature passes because xr+ks≡m(modp−1). The security aim is that someone without x cannot efficiently produce a valid signature on a new authenticated message. Nonce secrecy and freshness matter: reuse gives linear congruences relating two message hashes, the nonce and the secret key. Signing unhashed arbitrary messages also permits algebraic forgeries, so the hash is part of the practical scheme.

The independent Laplace distribution responses have log likelihood
ℓ(β,σ)=−nlog(2σ)−σS1​(β)​.
(5)
For every fixed positive σ, maximizing this expression means minimizing the sum of absolute residuals. Thus β​ is a least absolute deviations estimate, not a least-squares estimate. Such a minimizer exists: minimize the distance in the finite-dimensional closed column space of the design matrix. It need not be unique if the data or design allow multiple minimizers.
Write s=S1​(β​). For s>0, differentiating the profiled log likelihood gives −n/σ+s/σ2=0. Its unique maximum is
σ=nS1​(β​)​.​
(6)
If the fitted residual sum is zero, the likelihood instead increases without bound as σ↓0: there is no joint maximum with the stated positive scale parameter. The displayed estimate then denotes the boundary limit, not an admissible positive-scale MLE.
An ordinary exponential dispersion family has log density [yθ−b(θ)]/a(σ)+c(y,σ), so changing the mean changes the log density by an affine function of y. For two distinct Laplace locations μ1​,μ2​, their log-density difference is (∣y−μ2​∣−∣y−μ1​∣)/σ, with different slopes on the intervals separated by the two locations. It is not affine in y. Equivalently the kink at y=μ moves with the parameter. The Laplace location family is not an ordinary exponential dispersion family.

First-season recruits in year n+1 contribute ασγXn​. Seeds produced in year n−1 that survive two winters, fail first-season germination and germinate in their second season contribute βσ2(1−α)γXn−1​. Hence
Xn+1​=aXn​+bXn−1​,a=ασγ,b=βσ2(1−α)γ.​
(7)
This treats recruitment from older seeds as absent; otherwise the two-season recurrence would need further terms. The characteristic polynomial is r2−ar−b. For distinct roots,
Xn​=Ar+n​+Br−n​,r±​=2a±a2+4b​​,​
(8)
with constants determined by two initial values. For b=0,a>0, the recurrence is first order after the initial step; for a=b=0 it gives Xn+1​=0. These describe the zero-root degeneracies without interpreting 00 in the formula.
Since a,b≥0, ∣r−​∣≤r+​. The positive root is less than one exactly when a+b<1: the polynomial is nonpositive at zero, has only one positive root, and its value at one is 1−a−b. Therefore
σγ[α+(1−α)βσ]<1 ⟹ Xn​⟶0.​
(9)
This is the decay condition for the two-season seed-bank recurrence. The deterministic model describes expected or averaged abundance; literal eventual integer extinction requires that interpretation. A corresponding branching model with geometrically decaying expected abundance becomes extinct almost surely, since the probability of any surviving plants is at most the expected number.

Words: 245
7E OurBigBook.com
The simultaneous zeros are the origin and the four corners (±1,±1). The Jacobian matrix is
J=(−2xy1−y2​1−x2−2xy​).
(10)
At the origin its eigenvalues are 1,−1, with eigenvectors (1,1),(1,−1), so the origin is a saddle equilibrium of Poincaré index −1. At a corner J=−2xyI. Thus (1,1) and (−1,−1) are stable nodes; (1,−1) and (−1,1) are unstable nodes, all of index +1. Although the node eigenvalues coincide, the equilibria are hyperbolic and their stability follows from their strictly signed real eigenvalues.
The lines x=±1 and y=±1 are invariant and divide the plane into nine convex regions. A nonconstant periodic trajectory cannot cross any of these lines by uniqueness, and cannot be contained in one of them because one-dimensional autonomous flows have no nonconstant periodic solutions. It must therefore lie inside one region. The central region contains only the origin, whose index is −1; all other regions contain no equilibria. But a simple periodic orbit has index +1, equal to the sum of the enclosed equilibrium indices. Its interior stays in the same convex region, giving a contradiction in either case. There are no periodic orbits.
Away from the invariant lines, trajectory curves have the first integral
1−y21−x2​=C,
(11)
since both logarithmic derivatives equal −2xy. The diagonal y=x is the unstable separatrix of the origin, leading toward the two sinks; y=−x is its stable separatrix, coming from the two sources. The diagram shows these separatrices, the invariant lines and the direction field.

Near zero the integrand is asymptotic to tz−1/2, and at infinity it decays exponentially. The defining integral therefore converges and is analytic for Rez>0, by locally uniform domination, also allowing logarithmic factors for differentiation. Multiplication by the entire function 1/Γ(z) does not enlarge the domain of the unevaluated integral itself.
On Rez>1, subtract the two convergent integrals and use
et+11​−et−11​=−e2t−12​.
(12)
The substitution s=2t gives I(z)−ζ(z)=−21−zζ(z). Thus
I(z)=(1−21−z)ζ(z),​
(13)
first there and then wherever the two analytic continuations agree. The Riemann zeta function is meromorphic on the plane with its only pole a simple pole at one. The prefactor has a simple zero there, 1−21−z=(z−1)log2+O((z−1)2). It cancels the pole, giving I(1)=log2. Elsewhere both factors are holomorphic. The analytic continuation of I is entire; it is the Dirichlet eta function.

Set s=a(t)/a(tdec​). Free propagation in the homogeneous expanding universe redshifts frequencies by ν=νdec​/s and dilutes physical number density by s−3. Number conservation in corresponding frequency intervals gives
nν​(t)dν=s−3nνdec​​(tdec​)dνdec​,dνdec​=sdν.
(17)
Inserting the initial Planck spectrum, the factor s−2(sν)2 becomes ν2, while its exponent is hsν/(kTdec​). Hence
nν​(t)=c38πν2​ehν/(kT(t))−11​,T(t)=a(t)a(tdec​)​Tdec​.​

The shape is preserved even without collisions maintaining thermal equilibrium; it follows from redshift of an initially Planckian distribution.
For the total photon number density put x=hν/(kT). For the energy density include the energy hν of each photon. Then
n=αT3,ϵ=ξT4,​

where α=(8π/c3)(k/h)3∫0∞​x2/(ex−1)dx and ξ=(8πh/c3)(k/h)4∫0∞​x3/(ex−1)dx. Both integrals are finite positive constants. Thus n∝a−3 and ϵ∝a−4, with the extra power supplied by photon-energy redshift.

11G (Coding and Cryptography)

Words: 148 Articles: 1
Paper 2 OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 148
11G OurBigBook.com
For a discrete memoryless channel, its channel capacity in bits per use is C=maxPX​​I(X;Y). The Shannon second coding theorem identifies this with the supremum of rates achievable by arbitrarily long block codes with error probability tending to zero: every rate below C is achievable, and no rate above C can have vanishing error. The channel is used independently at each transmission, and coding rate is measured using base-two logarithms.
Let q be the probability of using the second input symbol. The second output symbol occurs with probability q/2, so H(Y)=h2​(q/2). The first input has deterministic output and the second has one bit of conditional output Shannon entropy; hence H(Y∣X)=q and
I(X;Y)=h2​(q/2)−q.
(20)
For 0<q<1, its derivative is 21​log2​[(2−q)/q]−1, which vanishes at q=2/5. Strict concavity of binary entropy makes this the unique global maximum. Substituting gives
C=h2​(1/5)−2/5=log2​5−2.​
(21)
Thus Shannon's theorem supplies operational coding rates arbitrarily close to this value from below, and rules out reliable transmission above it.

For fixed t, let B have the binomial distribution with parameters m,t. The Bernstein polynomial is fm​(t)=E[f(B/m)]. Continuity on the compact interval gives uniform continuity and a finite bound M=∥f∥∞​.
Given ϵ>0, choose δ>0 so ∣f(s)−f(t)∣<ϵ whenever ∣s−t∣<δ. Since E[B/m]=t and Var(B/m)=t(1−t)/m≤1/(4m), Chebyshev's inequality gives
∣fm​(t)−f(t)∣≤ϵ+2MPr(∣B/m−t∣≥δ)≤ϵ+2mδ2M​.
(22)
The bound is independent of t, including both endpoints. Taking the supremum and then letting m tend to infinity proves fm​→f uniformly on [0,1]. This provides the required polynomial-approximation theorem with its proof.

Ct​=∇⋅(D∇C)+F.​
(26)
After the initial point injection, F=0 and D=kC with k>0, so radial symmetry gives Ct​=kr−2(r2CCr​)r​. Total mass is 4π∫0∞​r2Cdr=4πM.
A spreading radius R and typical concentration obey CR3∼M and R2∼kCt. Thus R5∼Mkt. In the proposed ansatz this gives
α=52​,β=53​,γ=51​,C=M2/5(kt)−3/5f(ξ),ξ=(Mkt)1/5r​.​
(27)
Direct substitution, including the time derivative of ξ, gives
−53​f−51​ξf′=ξ21​(ξ2ff′)′.
(28)
Multiplying by ξ2 makes the left side −(ξ3f)′/5. Regularity and zero radial flux at the origin set the integration constant to zero, so ff′=−ξf/5. On the positive region f′=−ξ/5. Nonnegativity, compact support and continuity at its edge give
f(ξ)=10(ξ02​−ξ2)+​​.
(29)
Its normalization is 1=∫0ξ0​​ξ2fdξ=ξ05​/75. Therefore the spherical nonlinear-diffusion source profile is
f(ξ)=10(752/5−ξ2)+​​,r0​(t)=(75Mkt)1/5.​
(30)
The concentration and flux vanish at the free boundary, so there is no distributional flux jump despite the derivative kink. The solution satisfies the diffusion equation weakly across that boundary and classically inside its positive region. Its support shrinks to the origin as t↓0, and testing against a continuous compactly supported function gives the limit 4πM times its value at zero. This verifies the prescribed point injection as well as the mass normalization.

A canonical transformation preserves the symplectic form and therefore the form of Hamilton's equations for arbitrary Hamiltonians. In one degree of freedom,
dQ∧dP=(Qq​Pp​−Qp​Pq​)dq∧dp=[Q,P],dq∧dp.
(37)

Equivalently the chain rule gives [F,G]q,p​=[Q,P]q,p​[F,G]Q,P​ for arbitrary transformed functions, so the bracket and Hamiltonian dynamics are preserved precisely with this factor one. The condition also makes the Jacobian nonzero and hence supplies local invertibility; a global canonical change of variables additionally requires the stipulated global bijectivity on its domain.

16G OurBigBook.com
A deduction from premises Γ in propositional logic is a finite sequence of formulas, each an allowed logical axiom instance, a member of Γ, or obtained from earlier formulas by an inference rule, such as modus ponens. For example a Hilbert system can use the schemas p→(q→p), [p→(q→r)]→[(p→q)→(p→r)], and (¬q→¬p)→(p→q), with modus ponens as its rule. Its last formula is the conclusion. A finite deduction uses only finitely many premises. The completeness theorem for propositional logic says Γ⊨v implies Γ⊢v; together with soundness, syntactic consistency is equivalent to existence of a satisfying valuation.
For compactness, if Γ had no model, completeness would give a deduction of a contradiction. That deduction uses a finite subset of Γ, which therefore also has no model. Contrapositively, if every finite subset has a model, so does Γ.
Fix the given valuation on Q and let Lv​ be its collection of true literals. Suppose {s}∪Lv​ were inconsistent. For a complex irreducible representation, every central element acts as a scalar by Schur lemma. If the representation is faithful, these scalars embed Z in C∗. Every finite subgroup of C∗ is cyclic: if its order is m, all its elements satisfy zm=1, and the mth roots of unity form a cyclic group. Thus Z is cyclic.
The trivial group satisfies the conclusion immediately. Otherwise let G be a finite p-group with cyclic centre, and decompose a faithful representation as a direct sum of irreducibles using Maschke's theorem. The nontrivial cyclic p-group Z has a unique subgroup C of order p. Some component does not kill C, since otherwise the whole representation would kill it. If that component had a nontrivial kernel N, the kernel would be a normal subgroup and the allowed intersection theorem gives N∩Z=1. Every nontrivial subgroup of cyclic Z contains C, contradicting the choice of component. That irreducible component is faithful.
Finally the regular representation is faithful, since left multiplication by a nonidentity element does not fix the basis vector at the identity. A cyclic centre therefore supplies a faithful irreducible component of it. The first argument proves the converse, giving a finite p-group has a faithful irreducible complex representation exactly when its centre is cyclic.

An equivalent martingale measure is a probability law equivalent to the physical law under which discounted traded prices are martingales. The bond has constant price one, so no discount factor is needed here.
Order the four states as UU,UD,DU,DD. Equivalence requires positive probability in every state, since the physical product law has full support. Each stock has risk-neutral up probability 1/2, obtained by solving 1=(1+ϵ)p+(1−ϵ)(1−p). Thus all equivalent martingale laws are
(qUU​,qUD​,qDU​,qDD​)=(a,1/2−a,1/2−a,a),0<a<1/2.​

The two risky returns need not be independent under a pricing measure.
A replicating portfolio pays b+θS2​+φS3​, so its four payoffs satisfy
YUU​+YDD​=YUD​+YDU​.​

Conversely this condition suffices: take θ=(YUU​−YDU​)/(2ϵ), φ=(YUU​−YUD​)/(2ϵ), and choose the bond holding to match YDD​. The relation then matches the fourth state as well. Its unique price is (YUU​+YDD​)/2=(YUD​+YDU​)/2.
For the same-direction claim, the payoff vector is (1,0,0,1) and its price under q is 2a. Thus the possible strictly arbitrage-free prices fill (0,1) and the lower arbitrage bound is the infimum zero. It is not achieved by an equivalent measure, and pricing the nonnegative nonzero claim at zero would itself permit arbitrage by buying it. Its payoff is not replicable, since the displayed payoff relation fails. A buyer may pay a positive amount for its insurance against joint downward moves, for a view about dependence, or according to risk preferences. Under the stated physical independent law its expected payoff is 13/25, illustrating that a zero lower bound does not make the payoff economically worthless.

For fixed terminal time and fixed endpoint, use the maximizing form of the Pontryagin maximum principle. For dynamics q˙​=f(q,u,t) and running cost L, there are multipliers (p,p0​), not all zero, with p0​≥0, and Hamiltonian of an optimal-control problem H=p⋅f−p0​L. Along an optimum, q˙​=Hp​, p˙​=−Hq​, and the chosen control maximizes H over admissible controls almost everywhere. Fixed terminal state imposes no prescribed terminal value of p; fixed time imposes no free-time condition H(T)=0. The normal case scales p0​=1; abnormal extremals have p0​=0.
For this problem the normal Hamiltonian of an optimal-control problem is
H=px​u+py​v+k(uy−vx)−21​(u2+v2),k˙=0.
(65)
Maximization gives u=px​+ky, v=py​−kx. The costate equations give p˙​x​=kv, p˙​y​=−ku, hence u˙=2kv, v˙=−2ku. Nonzero velocities rotate at constant angular rate, and rotational symmetry permits u(0)=A, v(0)=0. For a closed path, 2k=2πn, with integer n=0. Then z(1)=A2/(2πn), so the required positive endpoint has n>0, A2=2πn and cost πn.
To prove a global minimum rather than only classify stationary extremals, write r=(x,y) and subtract its time average; this changes neither its derivative nor ∫(yx˙−xy˙​)dt. The resulting closed mean-zero path satisfies the periodic Wirtinger inequality ∫∣r∣2≤(4π2)−1∫∣r˙∣2. This follows immediately by its Fourier expansion: each nonzero mode of the derivative has squared multiplier at least 4π2. The Cauchy-Schwarz inequality now gives
1=∣z(1)∣≤(∫∣r∣2)1/2(∫∣r˙∣2)1/2≤2π1​∫01​(u2+v2)dt.
(66)
The argument extends to square-integrable controls by the periodic Sobolev/Fourier interpretation. Thus the cost is at least π for every feasible control. Equality is attained by
u=2π​cos(2πt),v=−2π​sin(2πt),x=2π​sin(2πt)​,y=2π​cos(2πt)−1​,z=t−2πsin(2πt)​.​
(67)
These satisfy every endpoint and have cost π. Therefore the minimum is π, an area-constrained quadratic control cost. The global inequality also prevents an overlooked abnormal candidate from lowering it; in fact an abnormal finite maximizing Hamiltonian of an optimal-control problem would force both linear control coefficients to vanish and then force zero velocity, incompatible with z(1)=1.

Write ∣m1​,m2​⟩ for product spin states, and J+​=J1+​+J2+​. A highest-weight state is killed by J+​. For s=2 the unique m=2 state is ∣1,1⟩. In the m=1 subspace, J+​ kills a∣1,0⟩+b∣0,1⟩ exactly when a+b=0. In the m=0 subspace it kills a∣1,−1⟩+b∣0,0⟩+c∣−1,1⟩ exactly when a+b=b+c=0. Normalizing gives
∣2,2⟩∣1,1⟩∣0,0⟩​=∣1,1⟩,=2​∣1,0⟩−∣0,1⟩​,=3​∣1,−1⟩−∣0,0⟩+∣−1,1⟩​.​​
(79)
The left states are coupled states and the right states are product states. Lowering commutes with particle interchange, so the whole spin-s multiplet has the exchange sign of its highest-weight state: +1 for s=0,2 and −1 for s=1, or (−1)s. Integer-spin identical particles are bosons; their spatial partial wave changes by (−1)ℓ under interchange. Symmetry of the full state therefore requires ℓ+s even.
For decay from total angular momentum one, coupling requires ∣ℓ−s∣≤1≤ℓ+s. The case s=0 forces ℓ=1 and violates Bose symmetry. For s=1, the allowed range is ℓ=0,1,2 and symmetry leaves ℓ=1. For s=2, the range is ℓ=1,2,3 and symmetry leaves ℓ=2. The identical particles' intrinsic parity product is +1, so total final parity is (−1)ℓ. Hence
PX​=−1: (ℓ,s)=(1,1),PX​=+1: (ℓ,s)=(2,2).​
(80)
This uses the stated massive-spin angular-momentum model; no additional restrictions for massless transverse vector particles have been assumed.

For a self-adjoint Hamiltonian operator bounded below, the Rayleigh-Ritz variational principle says E[ψ]=⟨ψ,Hψ⟩/⟨ψ,ψ⟩≥E0​. Expanding in energy eigenstates proves this, since the quotient is a weighted average of energies. Optimize a tractable trial family to obtain an upper bound on the ground energy.
If Hψ0​=E0​ψ0​, a regular trial error ψ=ψ0​+ϵη gives the exact cancellation
E[ψ]−E0​=∥ψ0​+ϵη∥2ϵ2⟨η,(H−E0​)η⟩​=O(ϵ2).
(81)
The linear terms vanish because (H−E0​)ψ0​=0. Here η is a fixed finite-energy direction, or is uniformly bounded in the quadratic-form norm. A Hilbert-space norm bound alone is insufficient for an unbounded Hamiltonian operator: a norm-ϵ admixture of an eigenstate with energy of order ϵ−2 can have order-one energy error. The usual quadratic-error claim therefore presupposes a controlled-energy perturbation.
For the first excited energy minimize the quotient on states orthogonal to the exact ground state. Alternatively diagonalize H in a trial subspace and use the min-max principle: its second Ritz eigenvalue is an upper bound for the second exact eigenvalue. An arbitrary trial function without either orthogonality or a min-max construction need not bound the first excited level.
The one-dimensional even potential has even ground state and odd first excited state, by the Sturm oscillation ordering. Choose the automatically orthogonal odd trial function ψa​(x)=Nxe−ax2/2, a>0. Integration by parts gives the kinetic numerator ∫∣ψa′​∣2, and the given Gaussian moments give
E1​≤E(a)=23a​+2a3​+4a215​.
(82)
For example, the kinetic factor is (I0​−2aI2​+a2I4​)/I2​=3a/2, while the potential factors are I4​/I2​ and I6​/I2​. Differentiation gives the unique positive minimizer a3−a−5=0. Thus
a≈1.90416,E1​≤E(a)≈4.67824.​
(83)
This is an upper estimate, not an exact eigenvalue. Improve it with odd polynomial-Gaussian trial functions such as (x+bx3)e−ax2/2, or a larger odd Ritz basis, and optimize the width. The parity restriction keeps all such states orthogonal to the even ground state.

(∂p∂S​)T​=−(∂T∂V​)p​.​

Neglecting changes in macroscopic kinetic and gravitational energy, the first law gives U2​−U1​=p1​V1​−p2​V2​. Thus U1​+p1​V1​=U2​+p2​V2​, so enthalpy is conserved. The irreversible process is not assumed isentropic.
Since dH=T,dS+V,dp and dS=(Cp​/T)dT−(∂V/∂T)p​dp, one has dH=Cp​,dT+[V−T(∂V/∂T)p​]dp. Therefore the Joule-Thomson coefficient is

The connection is torsion-free, so on a scalar ∇a​∇b​ϕ=∂a​∂b​ϕ−Γabc​∂c​ϕ is symmetric in a,b. A covector also carries a connection acting on its own index, and commuting derivatives gives curvature, generally nonzero.
Use the curvature convention [∇a​,∇b​]vc​=Rdcab​vd​, consistent with the identity requested in the PDF. Some texts define the opposite Riemann sign, reversing both formulas. Expanding the prescribed derivative combination of the Killing equation gives
0=∇a​Sbc​+∇b​Sac​−∇c​Sab​=2∇a​∇b​vc​−[∇a​,∇b​]vc​+[∇a​,∇c​]vb​+[∇b​,∇c​]va​.
(86)
The three commutator terms are [−Rdcab​+Rdbac​+Rdabc​]vd​=2Rdabc​vd​, by antisymmetry in the last two indices and the first Bianchi identity. Thus
∇a​∇b​vc​=−Rdabc​vd​.​
(87)
In flat Cartesian Minkowski coordinates this says ∂a​∂b​vc​=0. Hence all Killing fields are affine:
va=aa+ωab​xb,ωab​=−ωba​.​
(88)
The constant term gives four translations and the antisymmetric term six Lorentz generators, rotations and boosts. Conversely every such field satisfies the Killing equation.
For the static block metric, time derivatives vanish and g0i​=0, g00=−1/f. The Christoffel formula gives Γ000​=Γij0​=0 and Γ0i0​=Γi00​=(∂i​f)/(2f). The vector va=(1,0,0,0) has covector components v0​=−f, vi​=0. Its only potentially nonzero derivatives are ∇i​v0​=−∂i​f/2 and ∇0​vi​=∂i​f/2; spatial-spatial and time-time derivatives vanish. Their symmetric sums are zero, proving ∂t​ is a Killing vector field.

Hence the stated damping condition prevents shock formation at every finite time. Equality also avoids a finite-time crossing, although the derivative may tend to zero as time tends to infinity. One form of the Householder-John theorem is as follows. Suppose A=A∗ and A=M−N, with M invertible and W=M+M∗−A positive definite. Then the stationary iteration Mx(k+1)=Nx(k)+b converges for every initial vector exactly when A is positive definite; its iteration matrix is B=M−1N and convergence means spectral radius below one.
For a known positive definite system, design a splitting with M easy to solve, such as diagonal or triangular, and arrange M+M∗−A>0. The theorem then guarantees convergence. For example M=sI has W=2sI−A>0 when 2s exceeds the largest eigenvalue of A. In the converse direction, the discrete energy identity A−B∗AB=(I−B)∗W(I−B) explains the criterion: stable B gives A as a convergent sum of positive matrices, while positive A,W force every iteration eigenvalue inside the unit disk.

Divide the supplied scheme by ω and take
M=ωD​+L,N=(ω1​−1)D−U.
(104)
Then A=M−N, and M is invertible because it is lower triangular with positive diagonal D/ω. Symmetry gives U=LT, so
W=M+MT−A=(ω2​−1)D>0(0<ω<2).​
(105)
The Householder-John theorem therefore gives convergence.
For a direct spectral proof, let B=M−1N=I−M−1A. Expansion verifies A−B∗AB=(I−B)∗W(I−B). If Bv=λv with v=0, then
(1−∣λ∣2)v∗Av=∣1−λ∣2v∗Wv.
(106)
The value λ=1 is impossible since (I−B)v=M−1Av and A is invertible. Both quadratic forms are positive, hence ∣λ∣<1. The error obeys e(k+1)=Be(k) and tends to zero, proving convergence to the unique solution A−1b for every initial iterate. This is the successive-over-relaxation iteration, with no assertion of convergence at the excluded endpoints.
